changelog: feat: the last two figures from the BI report. ROW DENDROGRAM ON THE TAXONOMIC HEATMAP. The rows are clustered and reordered, with the tree in a left gutter, switchable back to abundance order. Average linkage on Euclidean distance between rows, computed on the same row-normalised values the colours show — so taxa group by their PATTERN across samples rather than by how abundant they are; clustering the raw values would just sort the rows by size again, which ranking them already does. The clustering itself is now one function shared with the sample dendrogram: written twice the two would drift, and two trees in one report that disagree about what clusters with what is worse than having only one of them. PREVALENCE FACETED BY GROUP. One panel per group, each recomputing prevalence inside its own samples, so a taxon found in both samples of a two-sample group reads 100% there and 50% overall — different numbers that are both right, which is why every panel header states its n. The panels share one x axis: on separate scales they would look comparable and not be. The single plot and the grid are drawn by the same function, so they can be read against each other. Two label fixes that came with them. (1) The taxon names beside the heatmap were cut at 22 characters and printed straight through the colour ramp; the ramp and the group key are now placed from the measured width of the longest name, the exported figure grows to fit, and the name is never shortened there — a row labelled "Christensenella...ae R..." names nothing, and the picture is what leaves the app. (2) On the facet grid the label de-collision walked as far as it needed and pushed names out through the top of their panel and across the title; a label outside its panel is read as belonging to the wrong group, so placement is now confined to the panel and a name with no room left is dropped rather than misplaced — fewer names, never a name in the wrong place. Tests: 15 drivers, 499 checks, against the real U2Bio-139-v144Genus result folder. The clustering is checked against the data rather than against a hard-coded order: each taxon's peak sample is read back out of the table view, and clustering must leave fewer runs of it than ranking by abundance does.
